Abstract 19 
Uranium is a toxic and pervasive geogenic contaminant often associated with soil organic matter. 20 
Its abundance and speciation in organic-rich permafrost soils are unknown, thereby limiting our 21 
ability to assess risks associated with uranium mobilization during permafrost thaw. In this 22 
study, we assessed uranium speciation in permafrost soil and porewater liberated during thaw 23 
using active-layer and permafrost samples from a study area in Yukon, Canada where elevated 24 
uranium concentrations occur in bedrock and groundwater. Permafrost contained 1.1–28 wt. % 25 
organic carbon and elevated uranium (range 7.6–1,040 µg g–1, median 25 µg g–1) relative to local 26 
bedrock. The highest soil uranium concentrations were encountered in catchments hosting 27 
uranium-enriched bedrock, and correlated positively with soil organic carbon. X-ray absorption 28 
spectroscopy, micro-X-ray fluorescence, and electron microscopy analyses revealed that uranium 29 
predominantly occurs as uranium(VI) associated with soil organic matter. Extended X-ray 30 
absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analyses suggested the presence of uranium(VI) coordinated 31 
with carbon, consistent with bidentate-mononuclear uranyl complexation on carboxyl groups. 32 
Permafrost thaw produced circumneutral pH porewater (pH 6.2–7.5) with elevated dissolved 33 
uranium (0.5–203 µg L–1). Geochemical modeling indicated that calcium-uranyl-carbonate 34 
complexes dominated dissolved uranium speciation. This study indicates that permafrost soil can 35 
mobilize uranium upon thaw, and that uranium fate is linked to dynamic biogeochemical 36 
reactions involving organic carbon and groundwater chemistry. 37
